cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of termination provisions and explain their advantages and disadvantages; identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction
cards.reading: Reading 94: Gregory, ISDA Master Agreement, Netting and Close-out
cards.statement: Events of default arise from a party's own failure, such as non-payment or bankruptcy, and generally allow the non-defaulting party to terminate all transactions; termination events are typically no-fault, such as illegality or a tax event, and may affect only the transactions concerned. Additional termination events tied to a rating downgrade create cliff risk, since they force close-out or collateral posting precisely when the counterparty is least able to fund it.
cards.explanation: Events of default are fault-based and permit close-out of the whole netting set; termination events are typically no-fault and narrower. Rating-linked additional termination events create cliff risk that can accelerate a counterparty's failure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of termination provisions and explain their advantages and disadvantages; identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction
cards.reading: Reading 94: Gregory, ISDA Master Agreement, Netting and Close-out
cards.statement: Events of default are no-fault occurrences such as illegality, while termination events arise from a party's own failure such as non-payment; additional termination events reduce risk unambiguously because they allow early exit before losses accumulate.
cards.explanation: The categories are transposed: events of default arise from a party's own failure, while termination events are typically no-fault. Additional termination events do not reduce risk unambiguously, because rating-linked triggers create cliff risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of termination provisions and explain their advantages and disadvantages; identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction
cards.reading: Reading 94: Gregory, ISDA Master Agreement, Netting and Close-out
cards.statement: Termination provisions are standardised and non-negotiable under the ISDA framework, so neither party can add triggers linked to credit quality.
cards.explanation: The ISDA Schedule exists precisely so parties can negotiate amendments to standard terms, and additional termination events linked to credit quality are among the most commonly negotiated provisions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the rationale for collateral management; describe the role of a valuation agent
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: Collateral management exists to reduce counterparty credit exposure to a residual level and thereby to free credit lines and support larger trading volumes; the valuation agent computes the mark-to-market of the netting set and the resulting margin call, and is typically one of the two parties, which is why disputes arise and why a third-party agent may be appointed.
cards.explanation: Collateral reduces exposure to a contractual residual and frees credit lines. The valuation agent computes exposure and the margin call and is usually one of the two parties, which is the structural source of disputes.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the rationale for collateral management; describe the role of a valuation agent
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: Collateral management exists to eliminate counterparty credit exposure entirely; the valuation agent is always an independent third party appointed by the regulator, which is why valuation disputes are rare in practice.
cards.explanation: Collateral reduces exposure to a residual level but does not eliminate it. Valuation agents are usually one of the trading parties, not regulator-appointed independents, and valuation disputes are common.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the rationale for collateral management; describe the role of a valuation agent
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: Collateral management exists primarily to generate funding for the receiving party through rehypothecation; the valuation agent's role is limited to custody of the posted assets.
cards.explanation: The rationale for collateral management is to reduce counterparty exposure and free credit lines; rehypothecation is only a possible consequence and is restricted for initial margin. The valuation agent computes exposure and the call, while custody is a separate function.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the rationale for collateral management; describe the role of a valuation agent
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: Collateral management exists to convert credit risk into market risk on the posted securities; the valuation agent is the custodian bank, which independently determines both the exposure and the eligible collateral schedule.
cards.explanation: Market risk on posted securities is a side effect of collateralisation, not its purpose. The custodian holds assets but does not determine exposure or the eligible collateral schedule, which is negotiated between the parties.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of collateral and the types of collateral that are typically used; differentiate between a two-way and one-way CSA agreement and describe how collateral parameters can be linked to credit quality
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: Cash and government securities dominate posted collateral, with corporate and equity collateral attracting larger haircuts; under a one-way agreement only one party posts, which is common where credit quality is asymmetric, whereas under a two-way agreement either party posts depending on the direction of the mark-to-market. Thresholds and independent amounts are frequently linked to credit ratings.
cards.explanation: Cash and government securities dominate because eligibility is driven by liquidity; riskier collateral carries larger haircuts. One-way agreements reflect asymmetric credit quality, and thresholds and independent amounts are often rating-linked.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of collateral and the types of collateral that are typically used; differentiate between a two-way and one-way CSA agreement and describe how collateral parameters can be linked to credit quality
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: Corporate bonds and equities dominate posted collateral because they offer a higher return to the poster; under a one-way agreement both parties post simultaneously to equalise exposure, while a two-way agreement restricts posting to the weaker party.
cards.explanation: Cash and government securities dominate posted collateral because eligibility is driven by liquidity rather than yield. Under a one-way agreement only one party posts; under a two-way agreement either party may post depending on the mark-to-market.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of collateral and the types of collateral that are typically used; differentiate between a two-way and one-way CSA agreement and describe how collateral parameters can be linked to credit quality
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: Only cash may be posted as collateral under an ISDA credit support annex, which is why haircuts are unnecessary; one-way and two-way agreements differ only in the frequency of margin calls.
cards.explanation: Securities are routinely posted under a credit support annex, which is why haircut schedules are negotiated. One-way and two-way agreements differ in who posts, not in call frequency.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of collateral and the types of collateral that are typically used; differentiate between a two-way and one-way CSA agreement and describe how collateral parameters can be linked to credit quality
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: Collateral type is prescribed by regulation and cannot be negotiated; one-way agreements are prohibited under the ISDA framework because they create an asymmetric credit exposure.
cards.explanation: Collateral eligibility is negotiated in the credit support annex within regulatory constraints, and one-way agreements are permitted and widely used; their asymmetry is an intended feature.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain aspects of collateral including funding, rehypothecation, and segregation; assess the impact of collateral on counterparty risk and funding, with and without segregation or rehypothecation
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: Segregation protects the poster by preventing the receiver from using the collateral, but it increases the poster's funding cost because the assets cannot be reused; rehypothecation reduces the funding cost by allowing the receiver to reuse the collateral, but exposes the poster to loss of the collateral if the receiver defaults.
cards.explanation: Segregation ring-fences collateral so it is returned if the receiver defaults, but locking assets away raises funding cost; rehypothecation creates reuse value but leaves the poster with only an unsecured claim if the receiver defaults.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain aspects of collateral including funding, rehypothecation, and segregation; assess the impact of collateral on counterparty risk and funding, with and without segregation or rehypothecation
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: Segregation reduces the poster's funding cost because segregated assets remain on the poster's balance sheet, while rehypothecation increases funding cost by removing the assets from circulation; neither affects counterparty risk.
cards.explanation: Both directions are reversed: segregation raises the poster's funding cost and rehypothecation lowers it. Both affect counterparty risk, since segregation exists to protect the poster against the receiver's default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain aspects of collateral including funding, rehypothecation, and segregation; assess the impact of collateral on counterparty risk and funding, with and without segregation or rehypothecation
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: Rehypothecation and segregation are mutually reinforcing: collateral that is segregated may still be rehypothecated, so the poster obtains protection and funding relief simultaneously.
cards.explanation: Segregation and rehypothecation are mutually exclusive for the same collateral: segregation is defined by the prohibition on reuse, so segregated collateral cannot be rehypothecated.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain aspects of collateral including funding, rehypothecation, and segregation; assess the impact of collateral on counterparty risk and funding, with and without segregation or rehypothecation
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: Segregation applies only to variation margin and rehypothecation only to initial margin, which is why initial margin is the cheaper of the two to fund.
cards.explanation: Initial margin is the type required to be segregated, which makes it the more expensive to fund; rehypothecation applies to variation margin where permitted.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various regulatory capital requirements
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: A bank holds default risk capital against counterparty exposure at default, computed under the standardised approach for counterparty credit risk or an internal model method; it separately holds a CVA capital charge for the mark-to-market volatility of CVA; and centrally cleared exposures attract a lower but non-zero charge, including capital against default fund contributions.
cards.explanation: Counterparty risk attracts two distinct charges, default risk capital and a CVA charge for CVA volatility, and central clearing reduces but does not eliminate the requirement.
cards.originalText: The bank holds default risk capital against counterparty exposure at default, computed under the standardised approach for counterparty credit risk or an internal model method; it separately holds a CVA capital charge for the mark-to-market volatility of CVA; and centrally cleared exposures attract a lower but non-zero charge, including capital against default fund contributions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various regulatory capital requirements
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: A bank holds a single capital charge against counterparty exposure at default, and CVA is excluded from capital because it is already reflected in the fair value of the derivative.
cards.explanation: CVA is not excluded from capital. Basel III added a dedicated CVA capital charge because CVA volatility caused most counterparty-related crisis losses without defaults occurring.
cards.originalText: The bank holds a single capital charge against counterparty exposure at default, and CVA is excluded from capital because it is already reflected in the fair value of the derivative.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various regulatory capital requirements
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: Capital is required only for uncleared derivatives; centrally cleared exposures attract no capital charge, since the CCP guarantees performance and the exposure is fully margined.
cards.explanation: Centrally cleared exposures attract a low but non-zero risk weight, and default fund contributions carry their own charge because they are mutualised and genuinely at risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various regulatory capital requirements
cards.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
cards.statement: The internal model method computes exposure at default as the sum of current exposure and an add-on prescribed by the regulator, which is why it produces the same result as the standardised approach for any given portfolio.
cards.explanation: Current exposure plus a regulatory add-on describes the current exposure method. The internal model method computes EAD as alpha times effective EPE from a simulated exposure profile, and results generally differ from standardised approaches.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities; explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact when there is correlation between transaction values
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: More frequent payments reduce exposure by resetting the accumulated mark-to-market more often, and an exercise date on an option truncates the profile because the position either terminates or converts; aggregating transactions under an enforceable netting agreement reduces exposure below the sum of the individual profiles, and the reduction is largest when transaction values are negatively correlated.
cards.explanation: Each payment resets part of the accumulated mark-to-market, exercise truncates the profile, and netting reduces exposure below the sum of individual profiles, most when transaction values move in opposite directions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities; explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact when there is correlation between transaction values
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: More frequent payments increase exposure because each payment date creates a settlement risk window, and exercise dates have no effect on the profile since the underlying risk continues regardless; aggregation reduces exposure most when transaction values are positively correlated.
cards.explanation: More frequent payments reduce pre-settlement exposure by resetting accumulated value; settlement risk windows are a separate short-dated risk. Exercise dates truncate the profile, and netting benefit is largest when values are negatively correlated.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities; explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact when there is correlation between transaction values
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: Payment frequency affects only operational cost and not the exposure profile, since exposure depends solely on the volatility of the underlying; aggregation has no effect on exposure unless the transactions are in the same currency.
cards.explanation: Payment frequency directly affects how much value accumulates between resets, so it changes the exposure profile. Netting also operates across currencies within a netting set when the agreement provides for it.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities; explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact when there is correlation between transaction values
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: More frequent payments reduce exposure, and aggregation reduces exposure by an amount that is independent of correlation, since netting is a legal mechanism rather than a statistical one.
cards.explanation: Netting is legally enabled, but its size is statistical: it depends on how transaction values co-move, and it is greatest when they are negatively correlated.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation; explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: In a CVA calculation, netting is incorporated by computing expected exposure on the netted portfolio rather than trade by trade, so that CVA is computed once for the netting set and allocated to trades through incremental or marginal CVA; collateral is incorporated by replacing the exposure profile with the collateralised residual, which is driven by the threshold, the minimum transfer amount and the exposure accruing over the margin period of risk, with segregated initial margin further reducing it.
cards.explanation: Netting changes the exposure profile that enters CVA, making CVA a netting-set quantity that must be allocated by incremental or marginal CVA; collateral replaces the profile with a residual governed by CSA parameters, the margin period of risk and initial margin.
cards.originalText: Netting is incorporated by computing expected exposure on the netted portfolio rather than trade by trade, so that CVA is computed once for the netting set and allocated to trades through incremental or marginal CVA; collateral is incorporated by replacing the exposure profile with the collateralised residual, which is driven by the threshold, the minimum transfer amount and the exposure accruing over the margin period of risk, with segregated initial margin further reducing it.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation; explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: In a CVA calculation, netting is incorporated by computing CVA trade by trade and then subtracting a netting benefit adjustment at the portfolio level; collateral is incorporated by setting expected exposure to zero for any netting set covered by a credit support annex.
cards.explanation: Netting enters CVA by simulating the netted exposure profile directly, not by adjusting trade-level CVAs. A CSA does not reduce expected exposure to zero; residual exposure remains from the threshold, minimum transfer amount and margin period of risk.
cards.originalText: Netting is incorporated by computing CVA trade by trade and then subtracting a netting benefit adjustment at the portfolio level; collateral is incorporated by setting expected exposure to zero for any netting set covered by a credit support annex.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation; explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: Netting has no effect on CVA because CVA is driven by the counterparty's credit spread rather than by exposure; collateral reduces CVA only to the extent that the collateral itself is credit risky.
cards.explanation: CVA depends on both the counterparty's credit spread and the exposure profile, so netting and collateral, which change exposure, directly affect CVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation; explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: Netting and collateral are both incorporated into CVA by applying a fixed regulatory multiplier to the uncollateralised CVA, since the alpha factor of 1.4 already reflects typical netting and collateral arrangements.
cards.explanation: Alpha is a regulatory capital multiplier applied to effective EPE, not a CVA pricing device; it does not substitute for modelling netting and collateral explicitly in CVA.
cards.originalText: Both are incorporated by applying a fixed regulatory multiplier to the uncollateralised CVA, since the alpha factor of 1.4 already reflects typical netting and collateral arrangements.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modelling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: In modelling wrong-way risk, hazard rate approaches make the counterparty's default intensity a function of the same variables that drive exposure; structural approaches link default to the counterparty's asset value; parametric approaches impose a simple functional relationship such as a multiplier on CVA; and jump approaches allow a discrete move in exposure or value at default, which is the only family that reproduces the limited effectiveness of collateral.
cards.explanation: The four families differ in how they link exposure to default; only a jump approach reproduces the discontinuous moves that make collateral ineffective against wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: Hazard rate approaches make the counterparty's default intensity a function of the same variables that drive exposure; structural approaches link default to the counterparty's asset value; parametric approaches impose a simple functional relationship such as a multiplier on CVA; and jump approaches allow a discrete move in exposure or value at default, which is the only family that reproduces the limited effectiveness of collateral.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modelling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: In modelling wrong-way risk, hazard rate approaches link default to the counterparty's asset value; structural approaches make the default intensity a function of exposure drivers; parametric approaches are the most flexible and require no functional assumption; and jump approaches are used only for equity derivatives.
cards.explanation: The hazard rate and structural descriptions are transposed. Parametric approaches are the least flexible because they impose a functional form, and jump approaches are not confined to equity derivatives.
cards.originalText: Hazard rate approaches link default to the counterparty's asset value; structural approaches make the default intensity a function of exposure drivers; parametric approaches are the most flexible and require no functional assumption; and jump approaches are used only for equity derivatives.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modelling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: The hazard rate, structural, parametric and jump approaches to modelling wrong-way risk all produce equivalent CVA figures for a given portfolio, differing only in computational cost, which is why the parametric approach is preferred in practice.
cards.explanation: Hazard rate, structural, parametric and jump approaches produce materially different CVA figures, particularly in the tail, which is why the choice of method matters.
cards.originalText: All four methods produce equivalent CVA figures for a given portfolio, differing only in computational cost, which is why the parametric approach is preferred in practice.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modelling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: Only structural approaches can capture wrong-way risk, because default must be linked to an economic cause; hazard rate, parametric and jump approaches are reduced form and are therefore incapable of generating dependence between exposure and default.
cards.explanation: Reduced form models generate dependence between exposure and default readily by making the default intensity a function of common variables; wrong-way risk modelling is not restricted to structural approaches.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: The principal pitfall of counterparty credit risk stress testing is excessive severity, since scenarios that are too extreme produce results management will not act on; the remedy is to calibrate scenarios to the worst outcome observed in the past five years.
cards.explanation: Counterparty stress scenarios are more often criticised for being insufficiently severe, and calibrating to recent observed history is itself a pitfall because the scenario can then never exceed what has already happened.
cards.originalText: The principal pitfall is excessive severity, since scenarios that are too extreme produce results management will not act on; the remedy is to calibrate scenarios to the worst outcome observed in the past five years.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: Counterparty credit risk stress testing duplicates the value at risk framework, so a bank operating a validated VaR model does not need a separate counterparty stress testing programme.
cards.explanation: Stress testing and VaR are complements: VaR is probabilistic and calibrated to historical distributions, while stress testing is scenario based and explores outcomes the distribution treats as negligible.
cards.originalText: The principal pitfall is that stress testing duplicates the value at risk framework, so a bank operating a validated VaR model does not need a separate counterparty stress testing programme.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the credit risks and other risks generated by retail banking; explain the differences between retail credit risk and corporate credit risk; discuss the dark side of retail credit risk
cards.reading: Retail and Sovereign Credit Risk
cards.statement: Retail portfolios are granular and statistically predictable, so idiosyncratic risk diversifies away and the residual is systematic; corporate portfolios are lumpy and require name-by-name analysis. The dark side of retail is that a new product's loss experience may look benign for years before deteriorating, so apparent stability can mask an unseasoned book.
cards.explanation: Large numbers of small exposures let idiosyncratic risk diversify away, leaving systematic risk, while corporate books need name-by-name analysis. Novel or unseasoned retail products can show benign early losses before deteriorating.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the credit risks and other risks generated by retail banking; explain the differences between retail credit risk and corporate credit risk; discuss the dark side of retail credit risk
cards.reading: Retail and Sovereign Credit Risk
cards.statement: Retail portfolios are lumpy and require name-by-name analysis, while corporate portfolios are granular and statistically predictable; the dark side of retail is that individual borrowers default unpredictably, which makes statistical modelling impossible.
cards.explanation: The characterisations are transposed: retail portfolios are granular and statistically modelled, while corporate portfolios are lumpy and need name-by-name analysis. Large numbers are what make retail statistical modelling possible.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the credit risks and other risks generated by retail banking; explain the differences between retail credit risk and corporate credit risk; discuss the dark side of retail credit risk
cards.reading: Retail and Sovereign Credit Risk
cards.statement: Retail credit risk is fully diversifiable because of the number of borrowers, so a granular retail book requires no capital beyond provisions for expected loss.
cards.explanation: Diversification removes idiosyncratic risk but not systematic risk. A retail book remains exposed to macroeconomic factors such as unemployment, house prices and rates, and capital is required for that.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the credit risks and other risks generated by retail banking; explain the differences between retail credit risk and corporate credit risk; discuss the dark side of retail credit risk
cards.reading: Retail and Sovereign Credit Risk
cards.statement: The dark side of retail credit risk refers to the operational risk of processing high transaction volumes, and it is unrelated to the credit performance of the portfolio.
cards.explanation: The dark side of retail credit risk is a credit phenomenon: deteriorating quality concealed behind favourable early loss data in unseasoned or novel products, not operational processing risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast foreign currency defaults and local currency defaults; explain the consequences of a country's default
cards.reading: Retail and Sovereign Credit Risk
cards.statement: A sovereign can create the currency in which local currency debt is denominated, so local currency default is rarer and is usually a choice made to avoid the inflation that monetisation would cause; consequences of default include loss of market access, a banking crisis, a severe output contraction and frequent political turnover.
cards.explanation: Because a sovereign can create its own currency, local currency default is a choice driven by the inflation cost of monetising and is rarer. Sovereign default brings loss of market access, banking crises, output collapse and political turnover.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast foreign currency defaults and local currency defaults; explain the consequences of a country's default
cards.reading: Retail and Sovereign Credit Risk
cards.statement: A sovereign can create foreign currency reserves through taxation, so foreign currency default is rarer than local currency default; consequences are limited to a temporary rise in borrowing costs, since sovereigns cannot be liquidated.
cards.explanation: A sovereign cannot create foreign currency; taxation raises local currency. Foreign currency default is therefore more frequent than local currency default, and its consequences are far more severe than a temporary rise in borrowing costs.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast foreign currency defaults and local currency defaults; explain the consequences of a country's default
cards.reading: Retail and Sovereign Credit Risk
cards.statement: Local and foreign currency defaults are equally likely, since a sovereign's ability to pay depends only on its fiscal position, and rating agencies therefore assign a single rating covering both.
cards.explanation: Local and foreign currency defaults are not equally likely: local currency debt can be serviced by creating money, while foreign currency debt depends on reserves and export earnings. Agencies therefore assign separate ratings.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast foreign currency defaults and local currency defaults; explain the consequences of a country's default
cards.reading: Retail and Sovereign Credit Risk
cards.statement: Local currency default has never occurred historically, which is why local currency debt is treated as risk free in capital calculations regardless of the sovereign's rating.
cards.explanation: Local currency sovereign defaults have occurred, Russia in 1998 being the best known. Treating local currency sovereign debt as risk free regardless of rating is a documented weakness of some capital frameworks.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative; explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: CVA prices the counterparty's default risk; DVA prices the dealer's own default risk as a benefit; FVA prices the funding cost of the uncollateralised exposure; MVA prices the funding cost of posting initial margin; and KVA prices the cost of the regulatory capital the trade consumes over its life.
cards.explanation: Each xVA term prices a distinct cost of running a derivative: CVA and DVA for counterparty and own default, FVA and MVA for funding uncollateralised exposure and initial margin, and KVA for regulatory capital. DVA is the only positive term.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative; explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: CVA prices the dealer's own default risk; DVA prices the counterparty's default risk; FVA prices the market risk of the position; MVA prices the cost of margin calls received; and KVA prices the counterparty's cost of capital.
cards.explanation: CVA prices the counterparty's default risk and DVA the dealer's own. FVA prices funding cost, not market risk; MVA prices the funding cost of initial margin posted; and KVA prices the dealer's own cost of regulatory capital.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative; explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: The xVA components are alternative names for the same adjustment, and applying more than one to a single trade double counts the cost of counterparty risk.
cards.explanation: The xVA components price distinct costs and are additive. The only recognised double-counting concern is the specific overlap between DVA and FVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative; explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term
cards.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
cards.statement: xVA applies only to cleared derivatives, since uncleared trades are fully collateralised under the margin rules and therefore carry no valuation adjustment.
cards.explanation: Uncleared derivatives are the origin of the xVA framework. They are not fully collateralised, since thresholds, minimum transfer amounts and the margin period of risk leave residual exposure, and initial margin creates the funding cost priced by MVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard; describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: Initial margin is defaulter-pays and sized to each member's own portfolio risk, so it aligns cost with risk taking and limits moral hazard; default fund contributions are mutualised and consumed after the defaulter's own resources, which spreads loss but weakens the link between a member's risk and its cost, so a CCP relying more heavily on the default fund creates greater moral hazard.
cards.explanation: Initial margin is defaulter-pays and risk sensitive, so cost tracks risk; the default fund is mutualised and weakens that link, so greater reliance on it increases moral hazard.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard; describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: Default fund contributions are defaulter-pays and sized to each member's own risk, while initial margin is mutualised across members; relying more heavily on initial margin therefore creates greater moral hazard.
cards.explanation: The roles are transposed: initial margin is the defaulter-pays, risk-sensitive resource, while default fund contributions are mutualised. Relying more on initial margin reduces moral hazard.
cards.correction: Initial margin is defaulter-pays and sized to each member's own risk, while default fund contributions are mutualised across members; relying more heavily on initial margin therefore creates less moral hazard.

changes.to: while default fund contributions are mutualised

cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard; describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: Initial margin is defaulter-pays and sized to each member's own risk, while default fund contributions are mutualised across members; relying more heavily on initial margin therefore creates less moral hazard.
cards.explanation: The roles are transposed: initial margin is the defaulter-pays, risk-sensitive resource, while default fund contributions are mutualised. Relying more on initial margin reduces moral hazard.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard; describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: Initial margin and default fund contributions are both mutualised, which is why central clearing eliminates counterparty risk for surviving members and why moral hazard is not a concern in a cleared market.
cards.explanation: Initial margin is not mutualised, and central clearing converts bilateral exposure into exposure to the CCP and its waterfall rather than eliminating counterparty risk. The mutualised default fund does create moral hazard.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard; describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: Moral hazard is absent from central clearing under any funding structure, because the CCP monitors member positions in real time and can close out a deteriorating member before losses arise.
cards.explanation: Real-time monitoring reduces but cannot eliminate moral hazard, and a CCP generally cannot close out a member before losses arise, since losses are already embedded in the portfolio when default occurs.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the concept of novation under central clearing; define netting, multilateral offset, and compression
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: Novation allows the original trading parties to renegotiate the terms of their contract, with the CCP facilitating the process.
cards.explanation: Novation does not renegotiate the trade: the economic terms are unchanged and only the counterparty changes, with the CCP substituted as counterparty to both sides.
cards.originalText: It allows the original trading parties to renegotiate the terms of their contract, with the CCP facilitating the process.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the concept of novation under central clearing; define netting, multilateral offset, and compression
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: Under novation, the original bilateral contract is replaced by two new contracts, with the CCP becoming buyer to the seller and seller to the buyer, so that the original bilateral agreement ceases to exist.
cards.explanation: Novation extinguishes the original bilateral contract and substitutes the CCP as counterparty to both sides, leaving the CCP with a matched book.
cards.originalText: The original bilateral contract is replaced by two new contracts, with the CCP becoming buyer to the seller and seller to the buyer, so that the original bilateral agreement ceases to exist.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the concept of novation under central clearing; define netting, multilateral offset, and compression
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: Under novation, the original contract remains in force between the two trading parties, with the CCP providing a guarantee that pays out only if one of them defaults.
cards.explanation: That describes a guarantee, not novation. Under novation the original bilateral contract is extinguished and replaced by two contracts with the CCP.
cards.originalText: The original contract remains in force between the two trading parties, with the CCP providing a guarantee that pays out only if one of them defaults.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the concept of novation under central clearing; define netting, multilateral offset, and compression
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: Under novation, the CCP takes an economic position in the trade, so that it retains directional market risk in exchange for the clearing fee it charges.
cards.explanation: Because the CCP takes opposite sides of both trades, its book is matched and it holds no directional market risk; it acquires market risk only if a member defaults and its book becomes unmatched.
cards.originalText: The CCP takes an economic position in the trade, so that it retains directional market risk in exchange for the clearing fee it charges.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of a loss waterfall; discuss the risks faced by a CCP and the ways it manages its exposures
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: In a CCP loss waterfall, the purpose of the defaulting member's initial margin is to act as a safeguard against that member's own potential losses, sized to cover market volatility over the period required for a swift liquidation of its portfolio.
cards.explanation: The defaulting member's initial margin is a defaulter-pays resource placed first in the waterfall and sized to cover close-out risk over the liquidation period, so the defaulter bears its own losses before any mutualised resource is used.
cards.originalText: To act as a safeguard against the defaulting member's own potential losses, sized to cover market volatility over the period required for a swift liquidation of its portfolio.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of a loss waterfall; discuss the risks faced by a CCP and the ways it manages its exposures
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: In a CCP loss waterfall, the purpose of the defaulting member's initial margin is to incentivise other members to participate in the auction process for reallocating the defaulting member's trades.
cards.explanation: Auction participation is encouraged through auction design and juniority rules on default fund contributions. Initial margin is a defaulter-pays resource covering close-out losses on the defaulter's own portfolio.
cards.originalText: To incentivise other members to participate in the auction process for reallocating the defaulting member's trades.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of a loss waterfall; discuss the risks faced by a CCP and the ways it manages its exposures
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: In a CCP loss waterfall, the purpose of the defaulting member's initial margin is to provide additional operational funding for the CCP in the event of a member default and subsequent market disruption.
cards.explanation: Operational funding comes from the CCP's own capital and revenues. Initial margin is a risk resource dedicated to covering close-out losses from the defaulter's portfolio.
cards.originalText: To provide additional operational funding for the CCP in the event of a member default and subsequent market disruption.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of a loss waterfall; discuss the risks faced by a CCP and the ways it manages its exposures
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: In a CCP loss waterfall, the purpose of the defaulting member's initial margin is to be mutualised across surviving members so that the cost of any single default is shared from the outset.
cards.explanation: Mutualisation is the role of surviving members' default fund contributions, later in the waterfall. Initial margin is defaulter-pays and sits first so that mutualisation is a last resort.
cards.originalText: To be mutualised across surviving members so that the cost of any single default is shared from the outset.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe, compare, and contrast various credit risk mitigants and their role in credit analysis
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: An SPV isolates assets from the originator's insolvency; a DPC is a highly rated subsidiary established by a dealer to transact derivatives; monolines and CDPCs are highly rated entities that sell credit protection without posting collateral. Their common limitation is that each transforms counterparty risk rather than removing it, and their high ratings proved fragile precisely when the protection was needed.
cards.explanation: SPVs, DPCs, monolines and CDPCs each repackage or concentrate counterparty risk rather than removing it, and the high ratings they relied on were correlated with the exposures and proved fragile when protection was needed.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe, compare, and contrast various credit risk mitigants and their role in credit analysis
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: An SPV is a highly rated dealer subsidiary; a DPC isolates assets from the originator's insolvency; monolines post full collateral against every position, which is why they proved resilient in 2008. Their common limitation is operational complexity rather than credit risk.
cards.explanation: The SPV and DPC definitions are transposed, and monolines were defined by not posting collateral, which is why their failure in 2008 was so damaging. Their common limitation is that they transform rather than remove credit risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe, compare, and contrast various credit risk mitigants and their role in credit analysis
cards.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
cards.statement: Monolines and CDPCs differ from SPVs and DPCs in that they take no credit risk at all, acting purely as administrative conduits, and their limitation is that they add legal cost without changing the economics of a transaction.
cards.explanation: Monolines and CDPCs exist precisely to take credit risk by selling credit protection; they are not administrative conduits.
